claims.text: Artificial Analysis reports that evaluating MiMo-V2.6-Pro cost $206.66 in total and $0.13 per Index task [^7].
Index v4.3.2 distributes its weight across four categories: Agents 30%, Coding 20%, General 30%, Scientific Reasoning 20% [^4].

First, repeat counts are wildly uneven: GDP.pdf and CritPt are run five times, Terminal-Bench 4.0, SciCode and AA-LCR three times, and the remaining five — AA-Briefcase, GDPval-AA, AutomationBench-AA, AA-Omniscience and HLE — exactly once each [^4].

Summing the published item counts across the ten evaluations gives roughly 9,750 single-pass tasks [^4]; $206.66 spread across them is about $0.021 each, and the published $0.1332 implies a divisor near 1,550 — about 16% of the tasks actually run.
Against that, Artificial Analysis states that it estimates a 95% confidence interval for the index "of less than ±1%", derived from more than ten repeats on certain models [^4].
Xiaomi reports MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 46.32 on the same index [^36], a figure Artificial Analysis does not display.
The high setting consumed 200M output tokens across the index run and cost $2.73 a task; xhigh consumed 240M and cost $3.74 [^16][^3].

95% half-widths computed by this article from the binomial standard error at p = 0.5 (p = 0.49 for HLE), using the per-evaluation item counts published in Artificial Analysis' Index v4.3.2 methodology [^4].

The measurement literature points the same way from a different angle: Miller's work on evaluation error bars concludes that a new evaluation needs roughly 969 questions to detect a three-point difference at 80% power, and that clustered standard errors can be more than three times larger than naive ones [^37].

Separately, semantically neutral prompt-format changes have been shown to move accuracy by as much as 76 points on the same model and the same items [^53] — a reminder that the quantity being averaged is not capability but capability-given-a-harness.
All figures above are from Artificial Analysis' own comparison page as of 23 September 2026, which states verbatim that "Both models score 46 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index."[^1]
AA-Omniscience separates these two tied models by 24 index points, 8 against 32.[^1]
For calibration: the leaderboard leader as of 23 September 2026 is Claude Opus 5.5 at 46, with GPT-6 Astra at 44 and Claude Fable 5.1 at 43.[^2]
Artificial Analysis publishes Grok 4.7's Omniscience components — 47% accuracy against a 29% hallucination rate, down from Grok 4.6's 34%.[^3]

Because Artificial Analysis defines hallucination rate as the proportion of incorrect answers out of all non-correct responses,[^2] an index of 8 is reachable either by a model that knows little or by a model that answers confidently when it does not know.
MiMo posts 76 output tokens per second to Grok's 39, but time to first answer token is 28.79 seconds against 0.85.[^1]
AA-LCR v1.1 is 100 questions over documents of 10k to 100k tokens and carries 5% of the index;[^4] the leaderboard puts MiMo at 86.3% and Grok at 77%, behind Kimi K3 at 88.7%.[^5]
Artificial Analysis published Grok 4.6 at 61 on 12 August 2026 [^34]; its model page reports 44 today [^35].

The cost metric moved with it: the same model on the same unchanged $2 input and $6 output rate card is reported at $0.84 per Index task in August and $1.86 in September [^34][^35], because the task set got harder and longer, not because anyone repriced anything.

This repository's own independent price instrument, which tracks the cheapest dollar-per-million-tokens buying each capability tier under a frozen method, has been flat at $0.13 per million tokens for the top three tiers since 8 August 2026 across 171 records [^52].

A third consideration cuts at the constituents themselves: Epoch AI audited a random sample of 48 Humanity's Last Exam questions and found 22 of them — 46% — carried substantial accuracy-altering errors, designating the benchmark Flawed [^38].

GPQA-Diamond was dropped because models had solved it [^27], Terminal-Bench 2.1 was saturated with current models clustering between 84 and 92 [^24], and the private held-out share more than doubled specifically to reduce the ability of labs to game evaluations [^27][^6].

Every input to that figure is Xiaomi's own price card: $0.43 per 1M input tokens and $0.87 per 1M output, blending to $0.18 per 1M tokens under Artificial Analysis' 7:2:1 cache-hit/input/output assumption, as of 23 September 2026 [^7].

The card also carries a 99% cache discount — $0.0036 per million tokens on a cache read — so on a harness with long shared prefixes, the blended rate is dominated by a term that encodes Xiaomi's storage policy rather than the model's competence [^7].

Artificial Analysis lists **1 API provider** [^7]; OpenRouter's endpoint list for the model returns exactly one, "Xiaomi," serving fp8 at 1,048,576 context with 99.994% single-day uptime as of 23 September 2026 [^8].
MiMo-V2.6-Pro lists $0.435/$0.87 per million tokens; MiMo-V2.6-Pro-UltraSpeed lists $4.35/$8.70 — exactly 10× — and publishes no rate limits at all, where Pro publishes RPM 100 and TPM 10M [^9].
Spot rates come from Vast.ai as of 22 September 2026: H100 SXM median $2.4002 per GPU-hour, H200 $4.3428, B200 $8.7526 [^11].

DeepSeek published one 24-hour window at 226.75 average nodes of eight H800s costing $87,072 against $562,027 of theoretical revenue, a 545% cost-profit margin, which is a 6.45× revenue-to-cost ratio and an 84.5% gross margin — a markup routinely miscompared to a margin [^12].

Separately, DeepSeek V4-Pro is served by 71 providers, with NVIDIA, Hugging Face, ZenMux and TokenGo listing a comparable trillion-parameter mixture of experts at the same $0.43/$0.87 — unaffiliated commercial hosts with no incentive to subsidise a Chinese lab [^15].

And Z.AI's interim results show gross margin moving from −0.4% to +24.6% while average API selling price rose approximately 101% — margin recovered by raising prices, not by deepening a discount, against R&D of RMB 2,131.2m and a net loss of RMB 2,072.0m [^13].

Xiaomi's own words scope the number precisely: "in less than 6 days, MiMo-V2.6-Flash and MiMo-V2.6-Pro completed 30 steps each with a cumulative total of approximately 750,000 trajectories, at training costs of around 850,000 and 2.62 million US dollars respectively" [^17].
The live dashboard puts the Pro run at $2,620,670 and splits it 43.5% training, 43.8% rollout generation, 12.7% grading [^18].

The model card reports 1.02 trillion total parameters, 42 billion active, 384 routed experts, and 30 trillion tokens of pretraining [^10]; the predecessor V2-Flash was pretrained on 27 trillion tokens [^19].

DeepSeek-V3's technical report gave 2,664K H800 GPU-hours of pre-training, 119K for context extension, 5K for post-training, 2,788K total, priced at an assumed $2 per GPU-hour for $5.576 million — with the explicit caveat that the costs "include only the official training of DeepSeek-V3, excluding the costs associated with prior research and ablation experiments on architectures, algorithms, or data" [^20].

Xiaomi flags the gap in the same announcement — "behind these 6 days lie half a year of foundational research accumulation and engineering trial and error" [^17] — and Luo Fuli, who leads MiMo, describes "a team of several dozen people" working through an era "when compute is brutally scarce" [^22].
Xiaomi reported FY2025 R&D expenses of RMB 33,132.2 million against revenue of RMB 457,286.7 million, with 25,457 R&D personnel [^21].
The widely repeated line that MiMo was trained "entirely on Chinese chips rather than Nvidia GPUs" traces to a named outside commenter, Daanish Khazi, not to Xiaomi [^22].
even against a backdrop where NVIDIA told the SEC it was "effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data center computing/compute market" as of fiscal 2026 [^23].

As of 22 September 2026 the corpus was not public — "the complete 7k+ task datasets have not yet been released" [^25] — and inspection of the XiaomiMiMo GitHub organisation on 23 September 2026 found 18 repositories consisting of a `verl` fork with four recipe directories plus `uni-agent` and `mimoagent`, with no RL-environment dataset repository [^26].
What is open is the harness and the recipes, under Apache-2.0 and MIT; the task corpus is the part that is closed [^25].

Why the RL-environment shape matters specifically: Cursor's sealed-container re-run of SWE-bench Pro removed runtime git-history leakage and found Opus 4.6 moved less than a point while Opus 4.8 Max fell 14.1 and Composer 2.5 fell 20.7, with 63% of Opus 4.8 Max's successes retrieved rather than derived [^30].
A 14.9-point relative swing between two versions of the same benchmark family, both legs run on Xiaomi's own harness [^10].

Terminal-Bench 4.0, released 26 August 2026, is a 66-task set with no task overlap with 2.1's 89, built by removing tasks that were saturated, refusal-prone, publicly solved, or affected by unresolved quality issues [^24].

The counterpoint is load-bearing and comes from the benchmark's own maintainers: cross-version deltas "mix genuine system progress with protocol changes," and 4.0 changed resources as well as tasks, so this is not a clean contamination readout [^24].

What makes the card credible rather than promotional cuts the other way: MiMo-V2.6-Pro loses to Claude Opus 5 on 10 of the 14 rows where both are scored, including DeepSWE v1.1 (71.9 against 74.0), Toolathlon-Verified (76.9 against 80.6) and OSWorld-Verified (82.0 against 83.4) [^10].
These are MiMo-V2.5-Pro to MiMo-V2.6-Pro, both measured under Intelligence Index v4.3.2, so they are directly comparable [^31].
Artificial Analysis offers a partial control: evaluations with private questions or answers account for 45% of Intelligence Index v4.3's weighting, up from 40% in v4.2 [^6][^27].

GSM1k found gaps of −8.0 for Yi-6B-Chat, −7.2 for math-shepherd-mistral-7b and −6.3 for phi-2, but −0.2 for gpt-4o, +2.2 for claude-3-opus and +3.8 for gemini-1.5-flash, concluding that "all frontier or close-to-frontier models... appear to perform similarly on both GSM8k and GSM1k" [^28].

A year-controlled rewrite found 16 models losing a mean 14.2 points on AIME-2024 but 7.1 on the uncontaminated AIME-2025 — only the roughly seven-point differential is the contamination estimate [^29].
The only other third-party number in existence is an Arena AutoEval score of 1628 on Code Arena — explicitly unranked, with zero human votes [^39].

Arena is candid about what that means: AutoEval substitutes a reward model's proxy votes for human ones, achieves above 90% pairwise accuracy only when the true gap exceeds ten points, and treats models within five points as statistically indistinguishable [^40].
On the board that does carry human volume, MiMo-V2.6-Pro is absent and the prior generation sits at rank 44 with 60,919 votes [^50].
A named practitioner running a personal held-out suite reported MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 38.8 against Claude Opus 5's 66.9 and GPT-6 Astra's 57.9 [^42] — a spread far wider than the index's 46-against-51.
A separate structured hands-on found MiMo matching Claude Opus 5 at 23 of 23 hidden checks across three small scoped coding tasks at roughly a thirty-fourth of the cost [^54].

The independent literature on this gap is unambiguous in direction if not in magnitude: NoLiMa tested 13 models all claiming at least 128k context and found 11 of them dropping below half their short-length baseline by 32k [^51].
| Aider polyglot | absent | Board frozen since late 2025 [^43] |

A confirmatory factor analysis across 591 language models and 12 tests found a dominant general factor with an average loading of 0.81, explaining 65.6% of benchmark variance, with a mean inter-test correlation of 0.73 [^55].

OpenRouter's request share for the week beginning 14 September 2026 put DeepSeek at 25.4%, Google at 18.6% and Anthropic at 2.7% [^46], against an index top ten dominated by Anthropic and OpenAI; OpenRouter itself states that its rankings "measure adoption, not quality."
Menlo Ventures separately estimates Chinese open-source models at roughly 1% of enterprise LLM API usage [^47].

Epoch AI's canonical measurement of inference-price decline — 9× to 900× per year depending on the capability milestone — is denominated per token at a fixed benchmark score, and says nothing about tokens consumed per task [^49].

A 2026 hedonic price index built from 21,024 posted prices across 3,208 models finds token-denominated prices falling at 0.506 log points per year while the task-denominated rate estimate is +0.470 with a confidence interval spanning zero — the author declines to treat its sign as established, and only the *difference* between the two rates is significant [^48].
The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is not a test. It is a weighted average of ten tests, chosen editorially, reweighted six times in a year, and reported as an integer.
Batching closes most of the gap: at roughly 128 concurrent streams the multiple falls to low single digits.
And for the first time in the series, no base checkpoint was released: V2.5, V2.5-Pro and V2-Flash all shipped base repositories, V2.6 did not [^10].

The MiMo-V2-Flash technical report describes over 100,000 code tasks derived from real-world GitHub issues, roughly 120K containerised environments in rollout, and more than 10,000 concurrent Kubernetes pods [^19].
Second, two of the ten constituents are Elo ratings linearly rescaled into the same average as pass-rate percentages, and frozen at the moment a model is added [^4].

That is not an error. Artificial Analysis defines cost per task as a *weighted* average across benchmarks, using the same weights the index uses [^4], so the "task" in "$0.13 a task" is a synthetic unit that corresponds to no workload anyone executed.
